newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Arsenic panic to aggravate diarrhoea in Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: Arsenic panic to aggravate diarrhoea in Bangladesh.

text.p: Growing panic in Bangladesh over drinking water contaminated with arsenic could aggravate another deadly health hazard -- diarrhoea, the World Bank said on Wednesday.
"People are being panicked and reverting to surface water from tubewell water, and becoming vulnerable to diarrhoea," Dr Babar Kabir, a World Bank water expert, told a news conference in Dhaka.
Diarrhoea already claims thousands of lives a year in Bangladesh.

"This is dangerous. Arsenic takes 10 to 15 years to claim a life but diarrhoea in days," said Kabir, the country team leader of the U.N. Development Programme (UNDP)/World Bank Water and Sanitation Programme.
Authorities in Bangladesh have sealed hundreds of tubewells after tests showed arsenic concentration above the World Health Organisation's safety level of 0.05 microgram per litre.
"We are not telling people to drink the water of those tubewells but people should be encouraged to drink tubewell water unless a permanent and sustainable alternative is found out," Kabir said.
"We don't want to lose a discipline (of drinking tubewell water) which saved hundreds of thousands of lives in Bangladesh," said Pierre Landell-Mills, the World Bank's country director in Bangladesh.
"Arsenic is a drinking water supply problem in Bangladesh, more than a health problem."
According to a recent patient identification survey, about 1,300 people in 24 of the country's 64 administrative districts suffer from chronic arsenicosis.
Those who drink water contaminated with arsenic can develop symptoms including, initially, black spots on their body and gradually lesions. If untreated, they can develop cancer.
World Bank officials said the UNDP would fund a $300,000 emergency programme, beginning this month, to provide immediate relief to the 200 villages worst hit by arsenic contamination.
All tubewells in those villages would be tested and the health of villagers in those areas screened before supplies of arsenic-free water are arranged, they said.
The British government would also fund a detailed ground water study programme from September to detect definite causes of arsenic pollution.
"Causes (of contamination) are still unknown. But we are expecting an explanation after the British study," said Kabir.

But he ruled out suggestions that the use of fertiliser and arsenic treated electric poles could have contaminated the water. "It's of purely a geological nature -- no links with fertiliser and pesticides," he said.

Landell-Mills said a World Bank expert team was due in Dhaka later this month to undertake a project for developing water treatment facilities in affected areas, and form arsenic free water supply options.
World Bank said the project size would be around $50 million, including contributions from co-financiers and the Bangladesh government.
